scoreNote: Strong (5): a recommendation-appropriate response that separates the circumstances in which free education is plainly beneficial from those in which a blanket promise is wasteful; relevant examples and a clear, qualified stance.

sentences.text: Few proposals wear their generosity as openly as the promise of a university education offered free of charge to every student who wants one.
Its champions argue that such a policy would throw open the doors of opportunity, dissolve the advantage of inherited wealth, and build a society both more skilled and more just.

I share the impulse behind the recommendation and believe governments should heavily subsidize higher education, yet offering it free to all students, in every circumstance, would be neither fair nor financially sound.
First, in a great many circumstances, removing the cost of education is unambiguously beneficial.

A gifted student born into a poor family, who could flourish at university but cannot begin to afford the tuition, is a loss not only to herself but to a society that will never receive the contributions she might have made.
Lifting that financial barrier converts wasted potential into doctors, engineers, and teachers, which is among the most productive investments a state can make.
The nations of northern Europe that fund higher education generously have reaped exactly this reward in the form of highly skilled and adaptable workforces.
Talent, after all, is distributed fairly evenly between rich and poor families, even though the opportunity to develop it is not.
Where money alone stands between a capable student and a degree, the case for free education is overwhelming.
However, the moment the policy is extended to all students regardless of need or ability, its logic begins to fray.

Wealthy families who could comfortably pay full fees would receive an expensive subsidy they do not require, financed by taxes that might otherwise have rescued poorer students or repaired crumbling schools.
Making education entirely free can also draw in students with little genuine interest in study, swelling enrolment, straining resources, and eroding the standards that give a degree its meaning.
Public money is finite, and every dollar handed to a student who could easily have paid is a dollar withheld from one who genuinely could not.
A policy that ignores circumstances ends up treating the desperate and the comfortable as though their situations were identical, which is the very opposite of fairness.
Finally, there remains the unavoidable question of who actually pays.
Free tuition is never truly free; it is financed from a public purse that must also fund hospitals, infrastructure, and the primary schools on which all later learning depends.
Whether the trade-off is worth making depends entirely on a country's wealth and on the priorities its citizens are willing to defend.
Citizens who applaud free college in the abstract may feel very differently once the cost arrives as higher taxes or longer hospital queues.
In a poorer nation, a grand promise of free university for everyone could quietly translate into overcrowded classrooms and underpaid teachers for the youngest children.
In conclusion, the recommendation is admirable in spirit but too absolute in form.

Governments should make higher education genuinely affordable and remove cost as an obstacle for everyone who needs help, but a blanket promise of free tuition for all, regardless of circumstance, is a blunt instrument poorly suited to a complex problem.
Affordability for all who need it, rather than free education for all who want it, is the wiser and more sustainable goal.
